question.prompt: A coin is altered so that the probability that it lands on heads is less than \(\dfrac12,\) and when the coin is flipped four times, the probability of an equal number of heads and tails is \(\dfrac{1}{6}.\) What is the probability that the coin lands on heads?

solutions.explanation:
Let \(p\) be the probability of heads. The positive probability of two heads and two tails rules out \(p=0\), so \(0<p<\tfrac12\).

Equal numbers of heads and tails in four flips means exactly two heads. There are \(\binom{4}{2}=6\) choices for their positions. Independence makes the probability of each such arrangement \(p^2(1-p)^2\), and the arrangements are disjoint. Thus
\[
6p^2(1-p)^2=\frac16.
\]
Since \(p(1-p)>0\), taking the positive square root gives
\[
p(1-p)=\frac16.
\]
Completing the square now reveals the two possibilities:
\[
\left(p-\frac12\right)^2
=\frac14-\frac16=\frac1{12},
\qquad
p=\frac12\pm\frac{\sqrt3}{6}.
\]
The plus sign gives a probability greater than \(\tfrac12\). The minus sign gives a positive probability less than \(\tfrac12\), so the answer is \(\boxed{\dfrac{3-\sqrt3}{6}}\), choice \(\boxed{\text{D}}\).
solutions.title: Count head positions and complete the square
